14.0.s.en: (1) The killing of John the Baptist

14.0.0.en: "At that time": during the preaching of Christ.

14.0.1.en: "Herod": this is Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great who killed the children of Bethlehem. He is the one to whom Pilate sent the Lord Christ to be tried before His crucifixion. He was ruler over Galilee, Samaria and Perea, which is the northern region of the land of the Jews. When he heard of the preaching of Christ, he thought that He was John the Baptist and that he had risen from the dead after he had killed him, because he feared John and his rebuke of him, since his words were the truth. "Tetrarch": the Romans divided the kingdom of the Jews into four parts, and set Herod Antipas as ruler over one of them.

14.1.0.en: Herod desired to marry Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, and he seized her from him while he was still alive, and no one was able to prevent him because of his authority and power. But John the Baptist, the man of the wilderness who fears no one because he relies on God, went in to him in his palace and rebuked him, and called him to leave Herodias and repent. But he did not repent, and he tried to silence John the Baptist and imprisoned him; indeed, he tried to kill him, but he feared the Jews because John was greatly loved and had a large following.

14.1.1.en: Do not try to silence your conscience and the voice of the Holy Spirit, but submit to it, for it will continue to condemn you if you do not repent, not only on this earth but forever in the final torment. So listen to His voice now and give up your desires, that you may rejoice forever.

14.2.0.en: Herod held a great celebration on the occasion of his birthday, which probably included food and much wine, and it was full of revelry and singing.

14.2.1.en: And the daughter of Herodias by Philip, who was called Salome, arose and danced a lewd dance to entice Herod. She did indeed entice him, to the point that he wanted to reward her at any price, even if he had to give her half of his kingdom. The wine he had drunk may also have helped fill him with lust and lack of balance, so he swore to give her whatever she asked.

14.2.2.en: Do not yield to lust, lest you lose your balance and your reason and become like the animals, and rush into words you will regret or deeds that defile your life.

14.3.0.en: Herodias had persuaded her daughter Salome of the necessity of getting rid of John the Baptist, because he hindered her from remaining queen through her marriage to Herod, and consequently she and her daughter would lose all the grandeur and wealth in which they lived. Indeed, it may have been Herodias who urged Salome to this lewd dance, so as to entice Herod and stir up his lust, so that she could ask him to kill John. Therefore, when Herod asked Salome what she wanted as a reward for her dancing, she answered at once, asking for the head of John on a platter, so that her mother would remain the wife of the king, and would obtain the whole kingdom and not only half of it.

14.4.0.en: When Herod heard that, he awoke from his heedlessness and was greatly grieved, either because he feared John and esteemed him, or because he feared the uproar of the people who loved John. But because of his pride, he could not go back on his oath, although it would have been better if he had humbled himself and refused.

14.4.1.en: And being a man of lust, he could not refuse the request of the daughter of his beloved, and he commanded that they cut off John's head and bring it on a platter.

14.4.2.en: Sin puts you in a predicament, but repentance makes you pure, so that you walk in uprightness and peace of mind.

14.5.0.en: They cut off John's head and brought it to the king, who gave it to Salome, and she presented it to her mother Herodias. Thus the wicked Herodias accomplished her purpose, but the voice of truth still rebukes her to this day, and will rebuke her forever while she is in hell.

14.6.0.en: "His disciples": that is, the disciples of John.

14.6.1.en: "Told Jesus": because their teacher John had urged them to follow Christ and to take refuge in Him in all their needs; their intention may also have been that Christ should beware of the wicked Herod.

14.6.2.en: The disciples of John were deeply grieved, and they went and took his body to bury it with honor, and informed Jesus of what had happened.

14.6.3.en: Thus ended the life of the angel who prepared the way for Christ, after he had proclaimed the voice of truth to all around him.

14.7.s.en: (2) The feeding of the multitudes with the five loaves and the two fishes

14.7.0.en: "When Jesus heard": that is, Jesus heard the news of the death of John, and that Herod was saying of Him that He was John risen from the dead.

14.7.1.en: "By ship": He boarded a ship from Capernaum to the eastern shore of the Sea of Tiberias. "A desert place": a valley near Bethsaida, which lies east of the Sea of Tiberias.

14.7.2.en: "Apart": His disciples, during that time, had been sent by Him to preach in the villages of Judea (Mk 6:30-31), and they met Him after He came out of the ship.

14.7.3.en: "The people heard": they learned that He had boarded the ship, heading to the east of the Sea of Tiberias.

14.7.4.en: "On foot": it seems that the wind was light, so they were able to catch up with Him after He reached the east of the Sea of Tiberias.

14.7.5.en: Jesus did not resist the evil of Herod, but withdrew to the wilderness, for He had a greater purpose, which was the accomplishment of redemption. He went to a desert place to teach us the importance of solitude and quiet in the lives of the children of God; it is an opportunity for spiritual fullness and self-examination, in order to go forth into service and the doing of good.

14.7.6.en: When the multitudes learned of it, they followed Him on foot, for He had become beloved by all, because of the greatness of His teachings, the abundance of His miracles, and His tenderness toward all.

14.8.0.en: "When Jesus went forth": He came out of the ship and met His disciples.

14.8.1.en: "A great multitude": the multitudes who arrived in succession from the cities and villages of Galilee.

14.8.2.en: "Was moved with compassion": that is, He had pity on them for their ignorance of the way of salvation and their preoccupation with their bodily needs, such as the healing of their diseases, yet they were ready to receive teaching.

14.8.3.en: Christ received the multitudes with love, healed their sick, and preached to them as was His custom. This was a preparation for them to eat the bread of blessing, just as a person prepares, through repentance and confession, by the healing of his spiritual diseases before partaking of the Holy Mysteries.

14.8.4.en: His care for the sick took a long time, since the multitudes numbered in the thousands, until evening came (the men among them numbered five thousand).

14.9.0.en: "Evening": the Jews had two evenings, the first in the afternoon, which is the one mentioned here, and the second after it, at sunset, which is the one mentioned in (v. 23).

14.9.1.en: The disciples took pity on the multitudes and thought that their Teacher was unaware of how late the hour was, so they alerted Him to send them away before darkness fell, especially since they had not eaten since the morning when they gathered around Him, because the place was desolate, outside the cities, with no food in it; and they forgot that Christ was with them, He who satisfies all and who had done many miracles, so how could it be hard for Him to feed them?!

14.10.0.en: The miracle of feeding the multitudes is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels, because it declares the blessing of Christ that covers all our needs, so that we rely on Him and do not worry about the disturbances of the world. Christ answered His disciples, asking them to give the people food to eat, so that they would take their place as those responsible for this people, and in order to test their faith: would they ask Him, that is, believe in His power, or would they submit to human logic and the lack of food?

14.11.0.en: "We have here": the disciples searched among the multitudes for anyone who had food, and found only this small amount, "five loaves and two fishes", because it seems that the multitudes thought they would return quickly, but the words of Christ and His miracles drew their hearts, so they stayed with Him until the end of the day.

14.11.1.en: "Five loaves": John (Jn 6:9) mentions that they found with a lad five barley loaves, which is the lowest kind of bread, that is, the food of the poor, but by the blessing of Christ it becomes abundant and satisfies all.

14.11.2.en: When Christ asked the disciples to feed the people, they did not think of returning to Him to satisfy them, but searched for any food among the people, and found only two fishes and five loaves, so they told Christ of their helplessness and presented to Him the little food they had found.

14.11.3.en: The five loaves signify the five books of Moses, or the five sacrifices of the Jews, and the five senses of man; they represent man's weak and limited capabilities.

14.11.4.en: "Two fishes": they signify the teachings of the Old and New Testaments.

14.12.0.en: Christ did not despise these weak capabilities, but asked for them to be brought so that He might bless them. However weak and little your spiritual striving may be, God awaits it attentively to bless it with His grace, and He will satisfy your whole life.

14.13.0.en: "On the grass": the valley in which they were sitting was a place for pasture and not for farming, so it was full of grass.

14.13.1.en: "Blessed, and brake": the loaf would be large and dry, so He broke it in order to reduce the crumbs of bread left after the meal.

14.13.2.en: And the blessing was either that the broken piece returned to its first size, so He would break it a second time, and so on... or perhaps that whenever He put His hand into the bag containing the two fishes and the five loaves He found others, or created others, and the distribution continued until all received, or in some other way; what matters is that they increased greatly until the multitudes were satisfied by the abundance of food.

14.13.3.en: Christ blessed the food after He had made them sit down quietly, and He lifted His eyes to heaven to teach them to pray before eating, asking for the blessing of God.

14.13.4.en: Then He gave to His disciples to distribute to the people in an orderly way, as Mark the Evangelist mentions (Mk 6:40) that the disciples made the multitudes sit in groups, each group of a hundred or fifty, for they are the priests of the New Testament responsible for shepherding and satisfying the multitudes, and so that no one would be forgotten, for order ensures that the food reaches everyone.

14.14.0.en: The blessing was so great that all the multitudes ate and were filled and there was left over, for God always gives generously.

14.14.1.en: Then He commanded that the fragments be gathered, out of respect and appreciation for the grace of God, and to show the greatness of the miracle, and the fragments filled twelve baskets, according to the number of the disciples.

14.14.2.en: And the carrying of the twelve baskets declares that what happened was not a dream or merely a feeling that the multitudes sensed, but a reality. Then, when they departed, they distributed these fragments to the poor whom they found in the villages through which they passed.

14.15.0.en: The number of the women and children was not mentioned, not out of neglect of them, but because the man is the head of the family and speaks for it. And symbolically, the women signify softness, and the children immaturity. A person should be strong and mature, not pampered.

14.15.1.en: And the number five thousand points to the five books of Moses, as we mentioned, and the thousand signifies heaven, that is, that the heavenly blessing of God covers all His children.

14.16.s.en: (3) The Lord Christ walks on the water

14.16.0.en: "Constrained": either out of compassion for them because of the weariness of the whole day, or because they felt, with the multitudes, that He was the awaited Messiah of whom Moses spoke. For Moses satisfied them with manna from heaven, and here is Christ satisfying them by His blessing from the two fishes and the five loaves. For this reason they tried to make Him king over them, that He might deliver them from the Romans, and the first to sympathize with this thought were the disciples, because of their love for Him; therefore He constrained them to depart. "To go before Him unto the other side": to cross from the east of the Sea of Tiberias to the city of Capernaum. After the miracle of feeding the multitudes, the crowds remained around Him to receive His blessing, to ask Him their various questions, and for Him to complete the healing of their sicknesses.

14.16.1.en: The disciples tried to help Him in organizing the multitudes, but He sent them away, to go before Him and cross to the other shore of the Sea of Tiberias. And when they tried to wait with Him, He constrained them to go for two spiritual purposes: (1) that He might be alone in the mountain.

14.16.2.en: (2) that they might face the trials of life and their weakness be revealed, so that He might help them with His power and strengthen their faith.

14.17.0.en: "He sent the multitudes away": this took a long time because of their attachment to Him, and in order to complete the healing of their sicknesses.

14.17.1.en: "The mountain": He went up to it to be away from the multitudes, and it was beside the valley in which they had gathered. One who seeks solitude for prayer tries to keep as far as he can from conversation with people and from many meetings, as some saints did, such as St. Anthony the Great.

14.17.2.en: "Evening": that is, the hour of sunset.

14.17.3.en: After Christ blessed the multitudes and sent them away, He went to be alone in the mountain. Thus He repeats the importance of solitude and quiet in our lives, especially before undertaking important works and services.

14.18.0.en: The disciples boarded the ship at evening time, and then night came. After a short while, contrary winds rose and hindered the progress of the ship; indeed, the waves beat upon it so that it almost sank, and the disciples, with their experience in sailing the sea, tried to advance the ship, but their attempts did not succeed.

14.19.0.en: The disciples remained in great distress until near the end of the night, that is, the fourth watch, which is the end of the period of darkness and about three hours before sunrise, that is, about four o'clock after midnight.

14.20.0.en: Before they fell into despair, Christ appeared to them walking on the water, coming toward the ship, and they were afraid of Him, for they supposed Him to be a strange spirit.

14.20.1.en: And here His divinity and His authority over nature were revealed for the second time, when He broke its laws and walked on the water (the first time was when He "rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm" ch. 8:26).

14.20.2.en: You too can be above the sea and its waves, that is, the world, if you believe and hold fast to Christ, so that you do not drown in your lusts, but rise above them through repentance.

14.21.0.en: Jesus reassured them, saying: It is I, Christ your Teacher. So the fear began to leave them as they heard His voice, which was familiar to them.

14.22.0.en: "If it be thou": this does not mean doubt, for Peter could not cast himself into death while doubting the person of Christ; rather it means, since You are Christ, grant me the grace of walking on the water. Peter believed in Christ who walked on the water, and in the impulse of his love he wanted to hasten to Him, so he asked Him to permit him to walk on the water that he might rejoice in meeting Him, and within himself he believed in Christ's authority over that. So Christ commanded him, saying: "Come." And he went down and walked on the water, rejoicing as he advanced toward Christ... Christ did not calm the waves, but gave him authority to walk above them.

14.22.1.en: Do not wait for Christ to remove the trial, for what matters most is that He gives you peace and faith, so that you are not troubled by it but walk above it.

14.23.0.en: Peter walked in faith while he looked at Christ, but when his gaze turned to the waves he felt their violence, and he was afraid and doubted his ability to continue walking on the water, and then he began to sink, and cried out for help to Christ, who stretched out His hand and lifted him, rebuking him for his little faith and doubt.

14.23.1.en: Fix your gaze on Christ in tribulation, and do not be troubled by its pressures, for He lifts you above it and keeps your peace.

14.24.0.en: After the disciples saw the authority of Christ over nature in His walking on the water, His permitting Peter to do so, and the sudden stilling of the wind when He entered their ship, their faith in Him was strengthened, and they declared this by worshiping Him, glorifying His greatness.
